s1.quote: The diveable wreck lies upside down at a depth of 58–68 metres (190–223 ft) in clear water.

s2.quote: now lies upside-down at a depth of 64m … Visibility can be so good – 20-30m-plus is not unheard of … Care must be taken around the wreck-site, because there is still a lot of unexploded ordnance … Diving Malin Head is strictly for the techies

summary.text: A WWI dreadnought mined in 1914 off Donegal, now resting inverted on the seabed in the open Atlantic. A deep technical dive with often excellent visibility, reached by boat from the Donegal coast.

s1.quote: at a depth of 98 to 131 ft (30 to 40 m) … Divers must obtain a licence from the Department … But large parts, such as her Scotch boilers, are still recognisable.

s2.quote: Lying in only 42m, the Laurentic might be overshadowed by the deeper wrecks in the area

s3.quote: Charted Depth: 41.8m … Badly broken up and scattered over a wide area. … Boilers are 5m high. … An ideal scooter dive. … Permission is required to dive this wreck.

access.value: Diving requires a licence/permission from the authorities

highlights.text: Scattered wreckage suited to scooter dive

hazards.text: Wreckage broken up and spread over a wide area

summary.text: A large WWI liner mined off Lough Swilly in 1917 and heavily salvaged for her gold. Now a broken, scattered wreck at about 40 m, with the boilers still easy to spot; a licence or permission is needed to dive it.

s1.quote: The ship settled at a depth of 5 to 20 meters (16 to 66 ft)

s2.quote: Charted Depth: 20m … Extensively broken up, she lies with her bow to the North East wedged in a gully. … Her twin boilers and her engine are the largest features. … Inhabited by some large congers. … Best dived 1 hour after High Water.

summary.text: A steamer lost on the Kedge Rock off Baltimore in 1916, now a broken wreck in a gully in about 20 m. A popular local dive best done around an hour after high water, with boilers, engine and congers to see.

s1.quote: The wreck lies at a depth 69 metres (226 ft). … largely intact except for a large blast hole

s2.quote: U-2511 (67 m) … She was scuttled on the 7th January 1946 and rests relatively intact.

summary.text: A Type XXI U-boat scuttled in Operation Deadlight in 1946 and still largely intact in the Atlantic off Donegal. A deep technical wreck at roughly 67-69 m, dived by expedition teams.

s1.quote: Patrick Valkenborgh giving scale to the bell of HMS Hurst Castle. … Malin Head, Ireland – 85 m/279 ft.
